<meta>continues from previous page: ...fur, or its dung, or have the plant <term>peristereon</term> <gloss>vervain or pigeon-herb</gloss>.</meta> A black stone, similar to a bean, is found in the Nile; when it is seen, dogs do not bark. You shall carry a dog’s tongue hidden in your shoe under your big toe, or if you carry a dog’s dried heart with you, according to Sextus; or hare’s fur, or dung, according to Pliny. Or you shall carry the severed tail of a young weasel on your foot, or give a frog to it in a morsel of food; all these things serve to escape the barking of dogs. Nigidius says that dogs will flee from the sight of anyone all day long who extracts a tick from a dog and carries it for a little while. Oppian:

> *But if you carry a small piece of a cut-up hyena skin,*
> *Suddenly the puppies and the fierce dogs*
> *Will be struck with bitter terror, and will not bark at you*
> *As you pass by hereafter, even if they were barking before.*

### *How to ensure a dog cannot run.*

If you smear its wings with oil, for it will be hindered in its running <note>The text likely refers to the legs of a bird or the movement of the animal; "wings" may be a metaphorical reference to the limbs in this context</note>, in this way it will come to pass.

### *How a hawk may be spirited.*

You will animate the bird against its prey, so that it attacks large birds; moisten the bait, which it uses during the time of hunting, with wine, or if it is a goshawk, give it a little vinegar. When you wish it to fly, give it three morsels of meat moistened with wine, or pour wine into a pigeon chick’s mouth from its beak, then make it fly. Thus:

### *You will make partridges more pugnacious,*

If you give them twigs of maidenhair fern <note>original: "adianti"</note> in their food, according to Pliny, and:

### *Roosters become more pugnacious,*

By giving them garlic in their food when they are about to fight. From this, in an old comedy, they are most wittily called <term>eskorodismenoi</term> <gloss>garlic-stuffed</gloss>, that is, someone fed on garlic, used for one who is vehement and too prone to battle.

### *So that a bird may not fly high,*

Pluck the feathers of the tail that direct the course upward; thus it will fly in a circle below. If you wish:

### *That a bird cannot fly,*

Cut the upper and lower tendons of the wing, and it remains without harm; the bird will not fly, and in this way, they do not escape in aviaries.

<summary>This page continues descriptions of various hunting and animal-handling charms, including methods to silence dogs, stimulate the aggression of hawks and roosters, and physically restrict the flight of birds.</summary>
<keywords>hunting lore, Oppian, Pliny, animal training, bird handling, pugnacity, folk medicine</keywords>

<meta>continues from previous page</meta>is distinguished by piety, religion, prudence, worship, and reverence of God, as if viewing the truth with the eyes of reason and trusting in his own faith, excelling among men as much as the sun surpasses the other stars with its light. For the sun itself illuminates the other stars not so much by the magnitude of its divinity as by its divinity and holiness. Therefore, believe this to be the second god, O Asclepius, governing all things and illuminating all living beings in the world, whether they are animate or inanimate. For if the world is a living being, always having been, being, and destined to be, nothing in the world is mortal. For in each living part that exists within the world, just as in one and the same living being that is always alive, there is no place for mortality. Therefore, God must be most full of life and eternity, if it is necessary for him always to live. The sun, therefore, is like the eternal world, and thus he is himself the eternal governor of vital things, or the companion and dispenser of all their vitality. God is therefore the eternal governor of the living, or of the vital things that are in the world, and the eternal dispenser of life itself. He has dispensed once by an eternal law, granting life to all vital beings in this manner, which I shall explain.

<summary>The text establishes the sun as the second god and eternal governor of all life within the world, arguing that because the world is a living being, nothing within it is truly mortal, and God serves as the eternal source and dispenser of this universal vitality.</summary>
<keywords>Asclepius, Hermes Trismegistus, sun, second god, vitality, eternity, governor, world-soul, life, divinity</keywords>

And there are things more wonderful than these: for on the Attic shore, the sea sounds like a zither. At Megara, a certain rock, when struck by angles, plays like a stringed instrument; so great is the power of Music. It soothes the soul itself, lifts the mind, incites combatants to war, and lightens the labors and weariness of individual tasks. It recalls the fallen and the desperate, and comforts travelers. And the Arabs say that camels carrying burdens are comforted by their singing guides. In a similar way, those carrying heavy loads sing, and are made capable and lightened by it: for song creates pleasure and capacity, mitigates the angry, makes the sad and anxious joyful, reconciles the discordant, and tempers the rage of the frenzied; it dissipates vain thoughts. For the truth is naturally good, joined together with life and light, and the avenger <note>referring to the forces of vice/darkness</note> did not approach beyond that point. Indeed, all the avenging powers were cast out by a certain sudden force. You have understood, son, the mode of this regeneration. Intellectual generation is composed by the presence of the number ten <note>the denary</note>, which rejects the number twelve. And we have contemplated this from the generation itself. Whoever, therefore, because of the benevolence of generation, which is according to God, loses his bodily sense, recognizes himself to be composed of divine things, and having become steadfast, he rejoices with the whole mind in divine power. **TATIUS.** O father, I conceive this not by the intuition of the eyes, but by the act of the mind, which is exercised through inner powers. I am in heaven, on earth, in water, in air. I am in animals, in trees, in a body, before a body, and after a body. But I would have you tell me this further: how are the avenging shadows repelled by the ten powers from the number twelve? What is the method, Trismegistus? **TRIS.** This tabernacle, O son, is constituted from the zodiacal circle, which consists of that number twelve. And there are eleven numbers, and one that is omniform according to the ideas of nature, for the wandering and circuit of man. Therefore, those avenging powers are in a way separated from one another, yet in their action they are in a way conjoined, as for instance, recklessness is inseparable from wrath. By right reason, therefore, they are deservedly separated to the extent that they are repelled by the ten powers, that is, by the number ten. The number ten, O son, is the generator of the soul. But life...

There are, therefore, gods who are the princes of all species; these are followed by gods whose prince is <term>ousia</term> <gloss>essence/substance</gloss>. These are sensible <note>perceivable by the senses</note>, having originated from both sources, and are like one another; they accomplish all things through sensible nature, each one illuminating its own work through another. The heaven, or whatever is understood by that name, its <term>ousiarches</term> <gloss>prince of substance</gloss> is Jupiter. For through the heaven, Jupiter offers life to all things. The <term>ousiarches</term> <gloss>prince of substance</gloss> of the sun is light. For the good of light is infused into us through the orb of the sun. Of the thirty-six stars <note>referring to the decans of the zodiac</note> (whose name is Horoscopii) always fixed in the same place, their <term>ousiarches</term> <gloss>prince of substance</gloss>, or prince, is he whom they call Pantomorphon <gloss>all-forming</gloss> or Omniform. He who, by diverse species, makes diverse forms. The seven spheres which are called erratic <note>wandering/planetary</note> have <term>ousiarchas</term> <gloss>princes of substance</gloss>, that is, their own princes, whom they call Fortune, <term>eimarmenēs</term> <gloss>fate/destiny</gloss>, by which all things are changed, with the law of nature established by the firmest stability, and varied by sempiternal agitation. Truly, the air is the organ, or machine, of all things, through which all things are done. But there is a second <term>ousiarches</term> <gloss>prince of substance</gloss> of this, for mortals things that are mortal, and things similar to these. These things, therefore, being such as they are, moving from the lowest to the highest, all things pertaining to themselves are naturally connected to one another, so that to mortals, mortal things are attached, and to sensible things, sensible things are attached. The sum of governance, however, obeys that highest Lord, so that it is not many, or rather it is one. For all things hang from the one, and rather flow down from it, although when seen from a distance they are believed to be many, divided. Yet, when unified, they are one or rather two, from whence all things are made and by whom they are made. That is, from the matter from which they are made, and from His will, by whose nod other things are effected. ASCLEPIUS: This, again, is the reason, O Trismegistus. TRISMEGISTUS: Such it is, O Asclepius. For God, whether as Father or Lord...

<keywords>Ousia, Ousiarchs, Jupiter, Sun, Pantomorphon, Fate, Eimarmene, Matter, Divine Will</keywords>

Indeed, arsenic certainly cannot be fixed at all, unless the operating artist has an equal knowledge of its coloring spirit, in which all philosophers have slumbered, attempting in vain to effect anything from it. Whoever, therefore, is ignorant of this spirit should have no hope of fixing it, nor of attributing to it the virtue by which it might acquire the perfection of transmutation. For this reason, I make it known to all that the whitening about which mention has been made is drawn from a false foundation, and that by it copper is falsely whitened, not transmuted. The sophists added Venus <note>original: "venerem"; the alchemical term for copper</note> thus masked and colored to its double in silver, and sold it to goldsmiths and minters; and finally, they transformed themselves into counterfeiters, not only those who sold it, but also those who bought it. Some of the sophists took red arsenic instead of white, and this itself departed into a false art. For in whatever way it is prepared, it exhibits nothing beyond whiteness. Some proceeded further, to common sulfur, which they cooked in this way with vinegar, lye, or very sharp urines, day and night, until it emerged white. Afterward, they elevated it from common salt and egg shells, cooked it by sublimation, and sublimated it, and that many times; it remained combustible nonetheless, although white. Yet by this means, to fix raw mercury...

<summary>The author explains why arsenic and sulfur cannot be truly "fixed" for the purpose of transmutation, exposing the deceptive methods of "sophists" who merely mask the appearance of metals rather than perfecting their inner substance.</summary>
<keywords>arsenic, sulfur, fixing, transmutation, sophists, Venus, copper, whitening, alchemy, sublimation</keywords>

Our material, however, is not bought from any shop, yet it is found there daily, and merchants throw it into the streets. It is therefore sufficient that it may be found for free. But the material of our <term>stone</term> is compared to all those things with which the practitioners labor. Indeed, our stone is <term>our salt</term>, <term>our mercury</term>, <term>verdigris</term>, <term>halonitrum</term> <gloss>a type of saltpeter</gloss>, <term>sal ammoniac</term>, <term>Mars</term> <gloss>iron</gloss>, <term>sulphur</term>, and infinite others of this kind, yet not dug out from wild, field-bound mountains with hammers and other instruments. But our stone is unearthed solely from our own mountains and fountains. In our <term>Salt-fountain</term> our <term>Salt</term> is found. From our earth our metal, <term>mercury</term>, and <term>sulphur</term> are poured, and not from wild, foreign, or field-bound mountains, all of which the practitioners do not understand, nor can they believe or comprehend. For the Lord has darkened and closed their senses, for which reason they used these things otherwise than they ought to have been used, and they did not aim at the target at all. Nevertheless, they persisted in this contrary sense and gave way to their own stubborn heads. Just as when they ought to have <term>distilled</term> gently, they <term>sublimated</term> with a strong fire there; they scorched the <term>aqua fortis</term> <gloss>strong water/nitric acid</gloss>, and they immediately burned up the operation of nature and the things themselves, reducing them to nothing. Likewise, when they should have <term>dissolved</term>, they <term>coagulated</term> there, and again, as those inexperienced in things, they handled the matter ineptly and fell into doubt, and with lying words they kept saying that the art was not true but false, in which, however, they lie by their own merit. For their own ignorance shamefully deceived them, a fact which must be attributed to their own dark, murky cunning, while, according to their obscure intellect, they interpreted words otherwise than they sounded. For example, when the Philosophers made words concerning <term>calcination</term> (which they call grinding), those unskilled <term>philosophrasters</term> <gloss>would-be philosophers</gloss> understood it as burning, and they reduced things completely to ashes, so that nothing could be made from them. 829. Since religion resides in the highest parts of a person, and from those highest parts his lower parts live and shine, and because Mohammed is involved in their minds together with their religion, therefore some Mohammed is always placed in their view. And so that they may turn their faces toward the East, over which is the Lord, he is placed below the Christian center. It is not Mohammed himself who wrote the <term>Alcoranus</term> <gloss>Koran</gloss>, but another who performs his duty; nor is it always the same one, but he is changed. At one time it was a man from Saxony, who, having been captured by the Algerians, became a Mohammedan; because he had also been a Christian, he was induced several times to speak with them about the Lord, saying that He was not the Son of Joseph, but the Son of God Himself. Others later succeeded this Mohammed. In the place where that representative Mohammed has his seat, a fire like a torch appears so that he may be recognized; but that fire is not visible to others than Mohammedans.

830. Mohammed himself, who wrote the <term>Alcoranus</term>, does not come into view today; it was told to me that in early times he presided over them, but because he wished to rule over all things of their religion as God, he was cast out from his seat, which he had held among the Papists, and sent down to the right side near the south. Once, a certain society of Mohammedans was stirred up by malicious spirits to acknowledge Mohammed as God. In order that the sedition might be quelled, Mohammed was brought up from the lower earth and shown, and then he was also seen by me. He appeared like a corporeal spirit, who lacks interior perception, with a face tending toward black, and I heard him speaking these words, *I am your Mohammed*; and soon he seemed to subside.

831. Mohammedans are hostile to Christians primarily because of the faith in three Divine Persons, and from thence the worship of three Gods, as many Creators, and furthermore to the Roman Catholics because of their genuflections before images; and from thence they call the latter idolaters and the former fanatics, saying that they make a three-headed God, and that they say "one" but whisper "three," and therefore that they divide Omnipotence, and out of one and a single Being they make three; and that they are like Fauns with three horns, one for each god, and together three for one, and that they pray thus, chant thus, and sound off from the pulpits thus.

832. Mohammedans, like all nations that acknowledge one God and love what is just and do what is good out of religion, have their own Heaven, but outside the Christian one. However, the Mohammedan Heaven is divided into two. In the lower one they live honestly with several wives, but from there no others are raised into the higher Heaven except those who renounce concubines and acknowledge the Lord our Savior, and at the same time His dominion over Heaven and Hell. I have heard that it is impossible for them to think that God the Father and our Lord are one, but that it is possible for them to believe that He rules over the Heavens and Hells because He is the Son of God the Father. This is the faith among them by which ascent into the higher Heaven is granted to them by the Lord.

833. That the Mohammedan religion has been received by more kingdoms than the Christian religion may be a scandal to those who think about Divine Providence and at the same time believe that no one can be saved except one who was born a Christian. But the Mohammedan religion is not a scandal to those who believe that all things are of Divine Providence; these inquire in what it consists, and they also find it. It consists in this, that the Mohammedan religion acknowledges the Lord as the Greatest Prophet, the Wisest of all, and also as the Son of God. But because they have made the <term>Alcoranus</term> the book of their religion, and from thence Mohammed, who wrote it, has settled in their thoughts, and they pursue him with some worship, they therefore think little of our Lord. In order that it may be fully known that that religion was raised up by the Divine Providence of the Lord to abolish the idolatries of many nations, it will be told in some order, but first concerning the origin of idolatries. Before that religion there was idolatrous worship.

OF OCCULT PHILOSOPHY,

### On the images of the head and tail of the Dragon of the Moon. Chap. XLV.

<note>A woodcut depicts a serpent or dragon coiled into a circular shape resembling the Greek letter Theta (Θ). The creature has the head of a bird (hawk) and a pointed tail. Within the circular body, there is a central vertical line crossed by a shorter horizontal line, with small astrological or symbolic marks at the terminals.</note>

They also used to make an image of the head and tail of the Dragon of the Moon, namely the figure of a serpent between a circle of air and fire, with the head of a hawk surrounding them, in the likeness of the Greek letter <term>theta</term> <gloss>Θ</gloss>. They fashioned it when Jupiter was holding the mid-heaven with the head <note>referring to the North Lunar Node</note>, which image they affirm contributes much to the success of petitions. By this image, they intended to signify a good and happy <term>daemon</term> <gloss>spirit</gloss>. They intended to represent him through the image of a serpent: for the Egyptians and Phoenicians celebrated this as a divine animal above all others, and they praised its divine nature because in it, above other animals, there exists a sharper and more expansive spirit. This is shown both by its swift movement without any feet, hands, or other instruments, and because it repeatedly renews its age and grows young again with <unclear>extraordinary</unclear> <note>the text likely intends "eximie," meaning remarkably or excellently</note> vigor. 

Indeed, they fashioned an image of the tail <note>referring to the South Lunar Node</note> in a similar way, when the moon was eclipsed in the tail, or afflicted by Saturn or Mars. They fashioned it for inducing anxiety and infirmity, and they called it an evil <term>genius</term> <gloss>spirit</gloss>. A certain Hebrew had enclosed such an image in a golden, double-linked belt, which Blanche, the daughter of the Duke of Bourbon, gave as a gift to her husband Peter, the first of that name, King of the Spains (whether knowingly or unknowingly). When he was girded with it, he seemed to himself to be encircled by a serpent. Having subsequently discovered the magical power inserted into the belt, he repudiated his wife for that reason.

### On the images of the Lunar Mansions. Chap. XLVI.

They also used to make images in the individual <term>mansions of the moon</term> <gloss>the twenty-eight segments of the lunar zodiac</gloss>. In the first, for the destruction of someone, they made an image in an iron ring of a black man clothed in sackcloth and girded, throwing a lance with his right hand. They sealed it in black wax and fumigated it with liquid storax and uttered imprecations. The matter in which <term>YHWH</term> <gloss>the Tetragrammaton</gloss> and <term>Elohim</term> <gloss>God</gloss> are praised is that they are performed through all the qualities, those that conclude with the quality of Judgment and those that conclude with the quality of Mercy. Just as you find in the creation of the first man, and in his judgment, and in his expulsion, and in all those matters, you will find that they all came about through the quality of Judgment and the quality of Mercy. Everything is in perfect completeness, in Mercy and in Judgment, all according to what is appropriate for true Judgment. According to this principle, the Torah said: "The Rock, His work is perfect" <note>Deuteronomy 32:4</note>. The interpretation of the verse is as follows: The Rock, who decrees judgment with strength, does not act in cruelty. He does not decree judgment except that "His work is perfect." Rather, the judgment that He decreed was previously deliberated between the two qualities, Loving-kindness and Judgment. This is the meaning of "His work is perfect," for the term "perfect" <term>tamim</term> is the secret of two things. It is as if it said "twins" <term>te'umim</term>, only in the language of honor, it speaks of two higher things using the term "perfect," and below it uses the term "twins." Thus, it says: "And they shall be twins below, together they shall be perfect at the head" <note>Exodus 26:24</note>. Below, they are "twins"; above, they are "perfect." This is because below they appear as two things, a thing and its opposite, as one assisting and one accusing. But above, everything is one intention. Whether assisting or accusing, both have one intention, and there is no hatred or love there, and no partiality, but only true justice. Therefore, it said: "His work is perfect," for in Judgment and in Mercy He deliberated and decreed the judgment, and this is the secret of true justice. 

As for what is said, "For all His ways are justice" <note>Deuteronomy 32:4</note>, it means that everything is for the eye of all who see, as it says, "For all His ways are justice." You already know that justice is inclusive of Judgment and Mercy, for justice corresponds to Jacob, who is the middle line <term>kav ha-emtza'i</term>, who mediates between the two tents, which are Abraham and Isaac. Abraham corresponds to Loving-kindness, Isaac to Judgment, and Jacob decides between them, "a plain man, dwelling in tents" <note>Genesis 25:27</note>. Justice corresponds to Jacob, drawing from Loving-kindness on the side of Abraham and from Judgment on the side of Isaac. Thus it says: "Justice and righteousness in Jacob You have performed" <note>Psalms 99:4</note>. The prophet said: "Correct me, YHWH, but with justice; not in Your anger, lest You bring me to nothing" <note>Jeremiah 10:24</note>. The interpretation of the verse is: "Correct me, YHWH, but with justice"—what it meant by "but" <term>akh</term> is a division, meaning: in half the quality of Justice, which is Loving-kindness. For Justice is half Judgment and half Loving-kindness. Therefore, it said "but with justice," and then it said, "not in Your anger, lest You bring me to nothing," revealing the secret to reduce the half of Justice that is from the side of anger. Therefore, Justice depends on Jacob, who is the patriarch of the tribes. He knew the great suffering of his children, when the Holy One, blessed be He, decrees upon them, so that he would request Mercy and righteousness for them. The secret is "And YHWH of Hosts shall be exalted in justice" <note>Isaiah 5:16</note>. What is written after it? "And the Holy God is sanctified in righteousness" <note>Isaiah 5:16</note>. This means: when Justice is exalted away from the rest of Judgment, it makes room for the quality of **El** <gloss>God</gloss>, which is the secret of what is said, "And the Holy God is sanctified in righteousness." In short, when YHWH of Hosts is exalted in justice, the quality of **El** comes, which is from above, and it performs righteousness, and the Justice is worked. This is the secret of what they said, that Justice is included in Loving-kindness and Judgment. As it says, "Justice and righteousness in Jacob You have performed." The great secret is "Righteousness and justice are the foundation of Your throne" <note>Psalms 89:15</note>, for righteousness is sometimes Judgment according to its reception of the abundance, as I explained that righteousness is great Judgment in strength. But when Justice participates with it, then the throne is established in Mercy. And if He is exalted in Justice, and reaches the Loving-kindness and Truth together—they are called the "Shining Countenances"—then everything is made into great Mercy, and this is the secret of "Let them go before..."

### **Torah** Light. These commandments mentioned in this portion are divided into three parts, which are the three pillars upon which the world stands: Torah, Worship, and Acts of Loving-kindness. Torah is the commandment of "You shall not add to it and you shall not take away from it," <note>Deuteronomy 13:1</note> which indicates the perfection of the Torah. And it is as the philosophers said: a thing that is perfect in ultimate perfection cannot be called lacking or excessive. For if it were lacking, it would not be perfect; and if it were capable of addition, it would imply it was not originally perfect. Therefore, the definition of the perfect is that it has neither lack nor excess. And it is known that the Torah depends upon His Great Name, which is Yod, He, Vav, He—the Torah of the Lord <note>original: "Torat HaShem"</note> is perfect, as I have elaborated upon this in my tractate *Shevuot*, in the chapter *Torah Or* <note>original: "Torah Light"</note>. And as it is written in the *Zohar* regarding this verse: "This is My name and this is My remembrance." <note>Exodus 3:15</note> *Yod-He* with "My name" equals 365. *Vav-He* with "My remembrance" equals 248. And it is written, "I am the first and I am the last." <note>Isaiah 44:6</note> And He is the Absolute Perfect; there is no deficiency in Him nor addition. And concerning this comes the warning: "You shall not do so to the Lord your God." <note>Deuteronomy 12:4</note> This is a warning against erasing the Name or shattering a stone from the Holy Temple. Behold, the letters of the Name are in the house where He, may He be blessed, dwells; and likewise the Temple. And it is written, "I am the Lord, My name is the..." The letters are like the closure for the house, and His Name, may He be blessed, is the soul for them. And one who destroys His house, as it were, destroys Him. This is the secret of "You shall not do so to the Lord your God." Worship is the majority of the commandments mentioned in this portion. And the command came to have a fixed, designated place in the Chosen House, and it said something with reasoning: "To His habitation you shall seek, and you shall come there." <note>Deuteronomy 12:5</note> "To His habitation" alludes to the <term>Shekhinah</term> <gloss>Divine Presence</gloss>, which is the palace of the name <term>Yod-Vav</term> <gloss>referring to the divine union</gloss>, as it is written... and as it is written: "Do not fear, for it is She who will dwell in me," <note>Refers to the sanctuary being the dwelling of the Presence</note> for in the Temple, the Glory is unified in the splendor of His people. And this is "To His name, His name there," as the <term>Targum</term> <gloss>Aramaic translation</gloss> says: "To make His <term>Shekhinah</term> <gloss>Divine Presence</gloss> dwell there." And around the place of holiness, the wicked walk, for they are the <term>Kelipah</term> <gloss>shell/force of impurity</gloss>. Therefore, "Take heed to yourself, lest you offer your burnt offerings in any place that you see." <note>Deuteronomy 12:13</note>

### **And** sometimes sparks of holiness spread outward, and it is a commandment to return them, to bring them inward. And this is the secret of the commandment to eat the firstborn and the sacrifice outside the city [and bring it] to the Chosen House. And then the branch returns to its root, and it is written concerning them, "There you shall bring up." <note>Deuteronomy 12:14</note> Meaning, there they shall have an ascent, and not outside. And since the Chosen House, which is in the Holy Land, is where the holiness is, therefore we were commanded to be "turn from evil" <note>Psalm 34:15</note> and to destroy all the places where the nations worshipped. And one must uproot and eradicate them, and this is commanded specifically in the Holy Land. And its secret is an allusion to the ten nations whose power is not [from] the worshippers of idolatry. And the matter is that the nations who are in the Land of Israel, under the rule of the Honored Name, worship God while "cutting the shoots" <note>A Talmudic metaphor for heresy</note>, and this is true idolatry. However, those in the lands outside the Land [of Israel] are under the rule of external forces. And just as there is a great prohibition to shatter one stone from the holiness, so conversely, it is a great commandment to destroy and eradicate a "bewitched city" <note>Biblical term for a city that has turned to idolatry</note> and not to build it again, for its place is impure. And likewise, one who entices and misleads, [one must] uproot and eradicate him, for he is from the impurity of the primeval serpent who was an enticer. And the Holy One, blessed be He, immediately said, "Cursed is the serpent," therefore there is no recovery for the powers of the enticer. And the commandment came not to love him and not to listen to him, as the matter said to the serpent: "And I will put enmity between you and the woman." <note>Genesis 3:15</note> Also a false prophet is like an enticer. Let us return to the matter: for the root of holiness is the Chosen House and Jerusalem. And this is the reason for first fruits, that the priests do not have permission to eat them until they are placed in the Chosen House. For the first fruits, which are the first-born, indicate great holiness, as I wrote in another place. Therefore, to the holy place they shall go, and from there they shall take their wisdom, for they are holy unto God, and they shall eat in Jerusalem. And the secret of the "lesser holy things" and the "second tithe" is that their consumption is in Jerusalem, and this is their grain, their wine, and their oil, which are the primordial fathers of all nourishment. And it is forbidden to eat the lesser holy things until after the blood is sprinkled. For the blood is the soul. And afterwards is the permission to eat and to enjoy. And know that just as the service, which is the sacrifice, is an offering to God, so is the one who serves, for the essence of the service is that he offers himself, in the secret of "When any man among you offers." <note>Leviticus 1:2</note> And the burnt offering is wholly consumed, for it comes because of a thought of "turning from evil," the thought which is spiritual, and he offers it all night... the serpent does not hinder him. And the lesser holy things are the perfection of the soul and the body.

### **And** the secret of the firstborn is the secret of the holy people of Israel, who are called as it is written, "Israel is My firstborn." <note>Exodus 4:22</note> And He spares them, "And you shall guard them," and they are called "the sheep of My pasture." Therefore, it is eaten only by the priests. And the secret of eating the holy things corresponds to [the fact that] they have blemishes and scars. For holy Israel—and Israel is called "Man" <note>Hebrew: Adam</note>—was a holy thing, afterwards a blemish fell upon him after he sinned and was clothed in "garments of skin." <note>Genesis 3:21</note> But he has a redemption in the secret of "And I will give a man in your stead." <note>Isaiah 43:3</note> And this was the secret of <term>Azazel</term> <gloss>the scapegoat</gloss>, "and [the goat] shall bear their iniquities." And let it be understood: their iniquities are those that fall upon his head and upon his people. But we were commanded not to cause a blemish in the holy thing in order to eat them, for [he] who causes a blemish in the holy things [does so] by his choice. Also [there is] the prohibition of work and shearing [the] holy things, for even broken tablets are holy.

### **The** conclusion of the matter: the service is the sacrifice, but the inner sacrifice is the man. And so his soul is called after his death to the altar on high, and Michael is the High Priest. And the principle is the secret that "in the image of God was man created." Therefore, the warning came to be careful in his life regarding taking of life, not to put a man to death except after thorough examination and interrogation. ### The Fourth Art

->Chapter Four: Regarding the Common Principles of Vomiting and Purging, and an Indication of How to Draw forth Laxative and Emetic Medicines<-

The person being purged should not hasten to consume many corruptible foods, lest the nature <note>natural faculties of the body</note> pull them down while they are undigested. If anything of this sort is required, it must be in small, measured amounts, gradually increased so that what enters the body is well digested. 

Venesection <note>the opening of a vein to let blood</note> is the specific evacuation for blood. As for evacuation specific to a humor that has increased in quantity or corrupted in quality, it is something other than venesection. Every evacuation that is excessive causes fainting in most cases. If the cessation of diarrhea—which the patient is accustomed to—results in an ailment, the recurrence of that evacuation usually remedies it, much like the way a nasal obstruction is relieved by inducing sneezing. Know that the remainder of the matter that requires evacuation is less susceptible to extraction, and persisting in it until the strength fails is ill-advised. Often, nature itself dissolves that remainder. As long as the humor is of the appropriate type and the patient can bear it, do not fear excess. Sometimes you may need to purge until the point of fainting. 

Whoever has great strength and a large quantity of corrupted humors should be purged little by little. This is also the case if the matter is highly matured or strongly mixed with the blood, such that it cannot be purged all at once. This applies to sciatica, chronic joint pain, cancer, chronic scabies, and chronic boils. 

Know that diarrhea draws from above and expels from below, so it is consistent with the familiar method of drawing. It is also consistent after the humors have settled; if the humors are from below, the method draws them towards it and expels them from where they are by the force of attraction, and vice-versa. The method of venesection varies according to the areas from which the blood is taken, as you have learned. Those who least need evacuation are those with good digestion, and inhabitants of hot climates have little need for it.

We say it is recommended for someone who wishes to be purged to vary or distribute their food intake. They should determine the amount intended for the day in one go, but make them different foods and different drinks. The stomach is often stimulated by this variety to desire to push what is inside it either upward or downward. As for food that is not varied but limited to one type, the stomach becomes satisfied with it, relaxes, and clings to it tightly, especially if the amount is small. As for laxatives, none of this is necessary. 

Know that the need for vomiting, purging, and the like does not arise in one who is well-regimented. Such a person requires only the mildest measures, and for them, exercise, massage, and cupping may suffice. If the body is filled to the greatest extent with the best of humors, namely blood, then venesection is what is needed for purification, not purging. When necessity dictates, purge or evacuate through methods such as those of autumn <note>a seasonal medical approach</note>. If a remedy can be achieved through vomiting, it is better than venesection; this is among the counsels of Hippocrates. This is also the case if phlegmatic humors are mixed with blood. However, if the humors are equal, viscous, and cold, venesection may increase their thickness and viscosity, so one must begin with purging. In general, if the humors are balanced, give precedence to venesection. If a purge is required later, let it be done. If they are not balanced, purge first until they become balanced, then perform venesection. Anyone who gave medicine before venesection should have performed the venesection first, even if only a little. Anyone recently venesected who requires a purge and drinks the medicine should have it paused. Frequently, drinking a laxative when venesection was required causes fainting and distress. If this is not calmed by sedatives, it is because venesection should have been performed first.

There is no evacuation that is needed because of extreme repletion except that the greatness of the ailment demands it, and repletion is according to quality and quantity. Often, good regimen takes the place of necessary venesection at the time. Often, the impetus for evacuation arises, but an obstacle intervenes; the only recourse then is fasting, sleep, and correcting the dyscrasia <note>imbalance of temperament</note> while managing the repletion. Some evacuation is by way of precaution, such as what is needed for those accustomed to gout, epilepsy, or other conditions at a known time, especially in the spring. It is necessary to take precautions before the time and perform the specific evacuation required, whether it be venesection or purging. Sometimes, the use of external desiccants and drying medicines acts as an evacuation, as is done with those suffering from dropsy. 

You may be forced to use a medicine that corresponds in quality to the humor being purged, such as scammony when you need to purge bile. In such a case, it is necessary to mix with it something that opposes it in quality but agrees with it in purging, such as myrobalan. Correcting the dyscrasia if it arises later in those with visceral tumors may weaken their purging. If you are forced to do so, use for them substances such as ivy or safflower. As for the laxative and cassia, that is what Hippocrates said: whoever has a constitution that easily responds to vomiting, the first step in their purification is to use vomiting in the summer or spring when the time is right, as that clears the body of fatigue. Know that one accustomed to a loose constitution or one unaccustomed to vomiting should avoid it when there is no need. 

It is necessary to prepare before purging by softening the humor one wishes to purge and dilating the passages at the time, as that clears the body of fatigue. Know that one who drinks, has a loose constitution, or is unaccustomed to vomiting, before using strong medicine, should follow a restrictive regimen. Purging while the intestines are weak is difficult and tiring. A medicine meant for vomiting may become a laxative if the stomach is strong, or if taken during intense hunger, or if the user has a loose constitution, or because of the nature of the medicine, or if the medicine is heavier in substance than what descends quickly. The laxative may be held back due to the weakness of the stomach, the intensity of the heaviness, the medicine causing distress, or the patient having indigestion. 

Every laxative medicine, if it does not purge when undigested, agitates the humor it is meant to purge and spreads it through the body. It then overcomes the body and draws other humors to it, increasing that humor in the body. Some humors are more responsive to vomiting in most cases, such as bile, while others are resistant to vomiting, such as black bile. Others have a state like milk and stars <note>obscure metaphorical or technical reference</note>, where purging is more appropriate. Whoever has a downward-moving humor, such as those with intestinal slipperiness, finds that contracting the intestines makes the laxative difficult. 

What is composed of medicines that are strongly different in the time of purging causes the purge to be disturbed; the first may purge the second before it has finished, or the first might purge the second itself. Anyone who experiences purging and has a clean body will suffer from colic and distress, and what is evacuated is evacuated with great difficulty. In general, a medicine that clears away morbid matter does not cause disturbance. If it is taken and there is disturbance, it is either purging things that are not morbid, or the humor being purged has changed, through vomiting or diarrhea, to another humor, which indicates the body has been cleansed of the humor intended for purging.

Be strong and let your heart take courage, all you who wait for the Lord.

A prayer of David. Incline Your ear, O Lord, answer me, for I am poor and needy. Preserve my soul, for I am faithful; save Your servant, O You my God, who trusts in You. Why, therefore, and in what manner does God foresee these uncertain future things? For if He deems that future things are inevitable, when it is not possible that they should happen otherwise, He is deceived; it is a crime even to think this, let alone express it. # Question

### The Third Article: Whether more universal things are prior in our intellectual cognition.

It is argued that more universal things are not prior in our intellectual cognition: because those things that are prior by nature are posterior and less known to us, but universals are prior by nature of our intellect. Furthermore, composites are prior in relation to us than simples. But universals are prior things: they are known later in relation to us. Furthermore, the Philosopher says in the first book of the *Physics* <note>Aristotle, *Physics* I.1</note> that the defined falls into our cognition before the parts of the definition and less universal things: just as "animal" is a part of the definition of "human," and universals are known later in relation to us. Furthermore, we come to know effects and principles by chance. But universals are known later in relation to us. But if it is as the Philosopher says in the first book of the *Physics*, one must proceed from universals to singulars. 

I answer that it must be said that in the cognition of our intellect, two things must be considered. First, that intellectual cognition takes its beginning in some way from sensitive cognition. And because sense is of singulars, and the intellect is of universals, it is necessary that the cognition of singulars be prior in relation to us than universal cognition. Secondly, it must be considered that our intellect proceeds from potentiality to act. And that which proceeds from potentiality to act arrives first at an incomplete act, which is the medium between potentiality and perfect act. The perfect act to which the intellect arrives is complete science, through which things are known distinctly and determinately; the incomplete act is imperfect science, through which things are known indistinctly under a certain confusion. For that which is known in this way is known as if in act and in some way in potentiality. As it is said in the first book of the *Physics*: the things that are first manifest and certain to us are more confused. Later, however, we know by distinguishing the principles and elements distinctly. It is manifest, however, that to know something in which many things are contained without having proper knowledge of each one of those things contained in it is to know something under a certain confusion. In this way, however, both a whole in which parts are contained in potentiality and an integral whole can be known: for either whole can be known in a certain confusion without the parts being known distinctly. However, to know distinctly that which is contained in the whole is to have cognition of a less common thing: just as to know "animal" indistinctly, and to know the animal in which is rationality or irrationality, which is to know a human or a lion. Therefore, it occurs first to our intellect to know "animal" and to know "human." And if I compare any thing, whether more or less, to how sense exits from potentiality into act, such is the order...

<column-break/>

of cognition appearing in the sense. For in sense one distinguishes more, and when a thing is known, it is known more remotely through <unclear>being corporeal</unclear>, and <unclear>being corporeal</unclear> and "animal," and it is known more as <unclear>being animal</unclear> and <unclear>being corporeal</unclear> and <unclear>that which is good</unclear>, and prior is <unclear>the good</unclear> and so on. Or it pleases, and it is clear that a child from the beginning distinguishes better and from the <unclear>better</unclear>; and in children, from the beginning, they call all men "fathers." Later, however, they terminate in each individual, as the Philosopher says in the first book of the *Physics*: as he who knows something indistinctly as yet and in potentiality, whether he knows it as a fiction or a principle, so he knows <unclear>genera</unclear> and can, so that he may know the <unclear>specifics</unclear>. And thus, by itself, indistinct cognition is the medium between potentiality and act. And thus, the cognition of singulars is prior in relation to us, and universal cognition is sensitive cognition and intellectual cognition. If it is both sense and with the intellect, cognition is more and is prior, and cognition is of the minor and the common. 

To the first, it must be said that through a double [way] it can be considered. In one way, through which it is considered according to the intention of truth. And since the intention of truth and the true is the same, it has a relationship to many things. It arrives and the abstraction of the intellect is the end here, while in truth it is posterior. In the first book of *De Anima* <note>Aristotle, *On the Soul*</note>, a universal is either nothing or is posterior: but he also placed universals as substances; and in this consideration, it is true: more so because particulars, when they are not, are only by participation in the subsisting universals which are called "ideas." In another way, it can be considered according to the nature itself of animality or humanity, as it is found in particulars. And thus there is a double order of nature. One is according to the way of generation and time, when those things which are imperfect and in potentiality are prior. And in this way, the more [universal] is prior in nature, which appears manifest in the generation of a human and an animal. For first, an animal is generated, then a human, as the Philosopher says in the book *On the Generation of Animals* <note>Aristotle, *Generation of Animals*</note>. The other is the order of perfection or the intention of nature, just as act is simply prior in nature, and that which is perfect is prior to that which is being perfected; and in this way, the less [universal] is prior in nature, for a human is an animal. Nature in its intention does not stop at the generation of an animal, but intends to generate a human. 

To the second, the more universal is compared to the less universal as a whole, and through the whole it becomes more universal, not only "animal" but also "human" and "equine"; as it can be [that the] less universal is contained in the future, not only the more universal but also others, like "human" not only as "animal" but as rational. Thus, therefore, "animal" considered in itself is prior in our cognition than "human." If "human" is prior in our cognition, then "animal" is so through its reason. 

To the third, it must be said that something can be known in two ways. In one way, absolutely, according to what it is in itself, and thus nothing is a house. In another way, when it is parts of this whole, and stones, it is necessary that we know the whole before the parts. For we know the house first in a certain confused way. Thus, therefore, it must be said that the defined, considered absolutely, is known before the definition. Otherwise, the defined would not be made known through those things. But the more universal [parts] are the parts.

When morning came for the Lion the next day, the Judge entered upon him along with a group of the prominent figures among his companions, carrying the document containing what Dimna had stated in his excuses <note>original: "معاذيره"</note>. The Lion took that document and ordered them to depart from him.

Then he sent for his mother and read that document to her. It weighed heavily upon her, and she said, "If I speak harshly to you, O King, do not be angry."

The Lion said, "I will not be angry, so say whatever you wish."

She said, "I do not see that you recognize what harms you from what benefits you. I fear that Dimna, through your prolonged hesitation in deciding his case, will incite against you a situation you will neither be able to sit through nor stand for."

Then she stood and left in a state of anger. When the next day arrived, the Judge sent for Dimna and brought him out. He consulted the scholars regarding him, but they said nothing about him.

The Judge then said to him, "Even if everyone who is present remains silent and says nothing, their suspicions have converged on the fact that you are a criminal, and there is no good for you in life after your guilt has been established in their hearts. I see nothing better for you than to confess your crime. By doing so, you will free your neck from the burdens of the afterlife, and a good reputation may return to you regarding your affair for two reasons. The first is your ability to find ways out and to fabricate excuses <note>original: "المعاذير"</note> that defend your person. The second is your confession of your sin, choosing safety in the afterlife over the safety of this world. For the scholars have said that death in what is honorable is better than life in what is disgraceful."

Dimna answered him and said, "Judges do not pass judgment based on their suspicions, nor on the suspicions of the common people or the elite. You have known that suspicion does not avail against the truth in any way. Even if you have all suspected that I am the author of this crime, I have certain knowledge of myself, and my knowledge of myself is a certainty in which there is no doubt. If my matter appears ugly to you, it is only because you have suspected that I strove [to commit this act]."

The tumult in the court of that king became manifest,
The hearts of the noble and commoners of the city were overcome.
With a conquering enemy seeking our ruin,
Or a disaster of the realm arisen from the unseen.
Which the jester had struck in his coarse haste,
A number of noble steeds were killed along the road.
Gathered at the palace of the king of the people,
Why did such haste and clamor appear?
From his urgency, the shouting was intense,
The clamor and confusion in the city of Tirmidh were great.
One man beat both hands upon his knees,
Another, from anxiety, was crying out and lamenting.
From the wailing, sedition, fear, and punishment,
Every heart was lost in a hundred kinds of fancies.
Everyone was casting omens based on conjecture,
Thinking: "What fire has fallen into the felt-cloth?"
He sought the way, and the King granted him passage quickly,
As he kissed the ground, he said: "Oh, what happened?"
Whoever asked about the condition of that morose man,
He placed a finger on his lip to signal: "Be quiet, hush!"
His suspicion fuels this behavior of his,
Everyone was bewildered and silenced by his anxiety.
The jester signaled so that the King of generosity,
Might grant a moment for me to catch my breath.
So that wisdom might return to the mind,
For I have fallen into a world of wonders.
After an hour, when the King, from suspicion and doubt,
Felt both his throat and mouth grow bitter.
He had never seen the jester like this before,
For there was no companion more pleasant than him.
He was always cracking jokes and pulling pranks,
He used to keep the King happy and laughing.
He would make him laugh so much in their sitting,
That he would clutch his stomach and belt.
That from the intensity of laughter, his body would perspire,
But today he is like this: sallow and morose.
Back, today, he is like this, sallow and morose,
Hand upon his lip, saying: "Oh King, be silent."
Suspicion upon suspicion, and fancy upon fancy,
As if the King, too, might expect punishment.
For the heart of the King was full of grief and caution,
Because the Khwarazm-Shah was very bloodthirsty.
He had killed many kings in that direction,
Through either guile or the power of that stubborn one.
This King of Tirmidh was in a state of suspicion,
And by the jester’s art, his suspicion was further increased.
He said: "Speak quickly, what is the situation?"
"Who is this turmoil and clamor of yours for?"
He said: "I heard in the village that the King,
Sent a herald to every crossroads."
"That I seek someone who will ride in three days,
To Samarkand, and if he arrives still..."
"I have packed corners and offered him in exchange,
Whatever benefit is obtained from the message."
"I hurried to go for that purpose,
But to say it—I do not have the strength."
"Such baseness should not come from someone like me,
Do not attach this hope to me."

<column-break/>

The state of all the people became broken and crazed,
The confusion of the elite and the commoners of the city doubled.
Or an overwhelming enemy appeared,
The jester arrived in a flurry of twists and turns.
Gathered there in the palace of the King of the people,
With obscene words and useless haste.
An old man was beating his knees,
The sedition and fear changed the countenances of the men.
In every thing, they were omen-casting and conjecturing,
Every heart was lost in a hundred kinds of fancies.
When the King gave him leave to enter his presence,
As he kissed the earth, he said: "Master, what is the news?"
Whoever asked of his condition with great effort,
He placed his hand upon his lips, meaning: "Be silent."
There, his suspicion grew beyond measure,
All were bewildered and struck dumb by his anxiety.
The jester signaled: "Oh King of generosity,
Give me permission so I may catch my breath."
So that wisdom might return to the mind,
For I have fallen into a wondrous state.
After an hour, when the King—his suspicion and doubt,
Having turned bitter and dry, for he was such a man—
Had never seen the jester so tense,
There was no one more playful and cheerful than him.
He was always engaged in jokes and witticisms,
He kept the King so happy and laughing,
That the King would double over in his hand,
And his body would sweat from the exertion of laughter.
And today he is like this, sallow and morose,
Hand upon his lips, meaning: "Be silent."
Suspicion upon suspicion and fancy upon fancy,
Would the King, too, fall into regret?
The heart of the King was full of grief and suspicion,
For the Khwarazm-Shah was a bloodthirsty ruler.
Many kings had been destroyed by that side,
Through the might or the guile of that stubborn one.
This King of Tirmidh was also fearful,
And the jester’s behavior added to that dread.
He said: "I have said in the village, oh King,
Whom does this clamor and malaise belong to?"
"I desire a person who, within three days,
Has given orders to the heralds for the sake of certainty."
"I would give treasures to him in return,
To go to Samarkand and receive the reward."
"I hurried for that very reason,
And once the purpose of the message is obtained,
"I do not have the power in me to speak,
Do not pin this duty upon me."

If you leave two sisters and a wife, and he bequeaths to a man the equivalent of a sister's share minus one-eighth of what remains of the estate after the bequest, the method for this is to set the basic division <note>original: "al-farīḍa"</note> at twelve shares. For each sister is a third of what remains of the estate after the bequest. This is an estate minus a bequest. You know that one-eighth of what remains plus the bequest equals a sister's share. So one-eighth of what remains is one-eighth of an estate minus one-eighth of a bequest. Therefore, one-eighth of an estate minus one-eighth of a bequest, together with the bequest, equals a sister's share; this is one-eighth of an estate and seven-eighths of a bequest. The whole estate equals three-eighths of an estate and three bequests and five-eighths of a bequest. Subtract three-eighths of the estate from the estate, and there remains five-eighths of the estate equaling three bequests and five-eighths of a bequest. The whole estate equals five bequests and four-fifths of a bequest. The estate is twenty-nine, the bequest is five, and the share is eight.

In another method of bequests: a man died and left four sons, and he bequeathed to a man the equivalent of one of his sons' shares, and to another a quarter of what remains of the third. Know that the bequest is only from the third.

Therefore, the Prophet, peace be upon him, said: "If a judge exerts himself <term>ijtihad</term> <gloss>independent legal reasoning</gloss> and is correct, he has two rewards; if he errs, he has one reward." And what judge is greater than one who judges concerning existence that it is such-and-such or not such-and-such? These judges are the scholars whom God has uniquely favored with <term>ta’wil</term> <gloss>allegorical interpretation</gloss>. **The Second Harm:** This arises from a friend of Islam who is ignorant. He thought that religion ought to be supported by denying every science attributed to them. So, he denied all their sciences and claimed they were ignorant in them, to the point that he denied their statements regarding solar and lunar eclipses, claiming that what they said was contrary to religious law. When this reached the ears of someone who knew those things through definitive proof, he did not doubt their proof, but he believed that Islam is built upon ignorance and the denial of definitive proof. Thus, his love for philosophy increased, and his hatred for Islam grew. A great crime against religion has been committed by those who think that Islam is supported by the denial of these sciences. 3223. There are two lights from which man is illuminated: the light of the world and the light of heaven. The light of the world is from the sun; the light of heaven is from the Lord. The light of the world is for the natural or external man, and thus for the things that are within him. Although the things therein do not appear as if they belong to that light, they nevertheless do, for nothing can be grasped by the natural man except through such things as exist and appear in the solar world, and thus have some form only by way of the light and shadow there. All ideas of time and ideas of space, which in the natural man matter so much that he cannot think without them, also belong to the light of the world. However, the light of heaven is for the spiritual or internal man. The interior mind of man, where his intellectual ideas—which are called immaterial—reside, is in that light. Man does not know this, even though he calls his intellect "sight" and attributes light to it. The reason is that, as long as he is in worldly and bodily things, he only has a perception of such things as belong to the light of the world, and not of such things as belong to the light of heaven. The light of heaven is from the Lord alone; the entire heaven is in that light. This light—namely, the light of heaven—is immensely more perfect than the light of the world. Things that form one ray in the light of the world form myriads in the light of heaven. In the light of heaven there is intelligence and wisdom. That is the light which flows into the light of the world that is in the external or natural man, and causes him to perceive the objects of things sensually. Unless that light flowed in, man would have no perception whatever, for the things that belong to the light of the world possess life from that source. Between these lights, or between those things that are in the light of heaven and those in the light of the world, there exists a correspondence when the external or natural man makes one with the internal or spiritual, that is, when the former serves the latter. What then exist in the light of the world are representative of those things that are in the light of heaven.

The longest day for the latitude of Jerusalem <note>original: "bayt al-maqdis"</note> is fourteen hours and some fraction, so the Jewish practice of using seasonal hours <note>original: "al-sa'at al-zamaniyya"</note> is not valid unless the conjunction <note>original: "al-ijtima'"</note> for the beginning of Tishri occurs exactly at the autumnal equinox <note>original: "al-i'tidal al-kharifi"</note>. It never occurs at that time, but rather precedes it or follows it by a significant amount, as we have clarified previously. 

When we determine the time of the conjunction through the calculation that the Jews provided in the table we analyzed based on their view, we proceed from there to the knowledge of the beginning of the year and how to determine its state of deficiency <note>original: "nuqsan"</note>, regularity, or completeness <note>original: "tamam"</note>. We have already attained knowledge regarding whether it is a simple year <note>original: "basita"</note> or a leap year <note>original: "kabisa"</note>. We then look in the table of limits <note>original: "jadwal al-hudud"</note> for a duration of days of the week <note>original: "ayyam al-usbu'"</note> whose boundaries contain the time at which the conjunction resulted for us, in the section for leap years if it is a leap year, and in the section for simple years if it is a simple year. When we find it, we find alongside it the beginning of the year from the week and its quality. Once we know the beginning of the year and its quality, and we combine that quality with the simple or leap year, we know from that the passage of the beginning of the next year.

Although it appears to have a color, everyone recognizes it is not like the color of our own bodies. Similarly, while it has flesh, bones, hair, and nails, it is not like that of any other living being. Even though it appears in such a way, it also causes all worldly beings to wonder. In this way, while that body exists as the very nature of a body, and while it appears as such and causes worldly beings to wonder, no one knows what its essence truly is. Thus, although it resembles the bodies of all, with all their shapes and forms, its nature is unknown. A body that is extremely radiant and extremely vast is called one that one cannot gaze upon enough. # The Commentary on the Noble Sutra of the Four Dharmas

Homage to Manjushri, the Youthful.

Why was this sutra composed, which states, "A <term>bodhisattva</term> <gloss>enlightenment-being</gloss>, a great being, should not abandon these four dharmas, even at the cost of his life, for as long as he lives"? It was composed to provide correct instruction to those who are confused about the methods for attaining supreme enlightenment after having entered the Great Vehicle; to ensure that those who are heedless correctly uphold these practices; to uplift those who are discouraged; and to bring joy to those who have already entered the path correctly.

Specifying the number as "four" is done to prevent the subject from becoming too expansive, which might lead people to lose interest, and to facilitate easier recollection.

Regarding the patience and kindness that appear below, they are not separate, as they share the same purpose. Although there are many classifications for those who have entered the Great Vehicle, only two names are mentioned here due to three causes: aspiration, practice, and realization.

What does aspiration mean? One is a <term>bodhisattva</term> <gloss>enlightenment-being</gloss> because one aspires toward profound objects of knowledge. One is a "great being" because one aspires to great power.

What does practice mean? It means one is diligent in attaining supreme, perfect enlightenment for oneself, and one strives to liberate all sentient beings from suffering.

What does realization mean? It means one realizes enlightenment through two powers. What are these two? They are the power of wisdom and the power of diligence. Without wisdom and with little diligence, it is impossible to realize enlightenment. For as long as one lives,

<margin>Poison even in the best things.</margin>
Who is there who would dare to deny that poison hides and exists even in the best things? All are compelled to confess this. If this, therefore, is true, I ask you now: should poison not be separated from the good and the useful? And the good taken, and the evil left behind? Indeed, it ought to be so. If, therefore, it ought to be: I pray, tell me, how is that separated in your workshops? For with you, everything remains mixed. But to defend your simplicity, if you are convicted to confess that poison hides there and you are asked where it finally goes, then you offer something or other about corrections, which claim to extract and remove the poison,
<margin>The correction of physicians is scrutinized.</margin>
just as they correct Quince with Scammony, or after Diagridium. But what kind of correction is that? Does the poison not remain afterwards just as it was at first? And yet you boast in the meantime that you have corrected it, so that the poison no longer harms. But where has it gone? 
<margin>Diagridion.</margin>
It remains in the Diagridium. Test that, if you are wise: exceed the measure, and you will see where the poison is. For you will know that not sluggishly. Thus you also correct Turbith, and call it Diaturbith. Such are your corrections, which would befit rustics and should be fed to horses. Make a trial by exceeding the measure and increase the dose; you will see if you will not feel the poison. 
<margin>What it means to correct as a physician</margin>
*To correct is to take the corrected.* Whoever is malicious and has sinned, if he is punished, the correction does not extend further than the will of the person who has been punished lasts. Such are these corrections too; it is placed with them, not with you. Now, in this case, a physician must consider nothing more than that the poison be taken away. This must be done through separation. As, for example: a serpent is poisonous, and yet it is adopted into food. If you take the poison away from it, you may eat it with no harm. The same must be understood equally regarding all other things; namely, that there is a need for a similar separation. That not having been done, you cannot be sure of your operation, unless perhaps it happens that nature supplies your deficiencies, or the greater beneficence of the heavens favors you. For in your art, no protection will remain.

Now, therefore, finally, if that true foundation which removes poison is necessary, how does Alchemy achieve it? For it is necessary that this be done so that, if Mars is in the Sun, Mars must be removed; and if Saturn is in Venus, it must be separated from it. For as many ascendants and impressions as there are in the things of nature, so many bodies exist within them. But those bodies that are contrary must by all means have something removed and taken away, so that by this pact all contrariety may be lifted, and the evil that you seek may be removed from the good.
<margin>Fire perfects all things.</margin>
As gold is useless for nothing unless it is first cast into the fire: so much less useful is medicine that does not pass through the fire. For it is necessary that all things pass through fire into another generation, which ought to conduce to and help man. And should this not justly be considered the sound foundation of any physician? For a physician ought not to employ poisons, but true <term>arcana</term> <gloss>hidden secrets</gloss>.

**T**here is, therefore, in all metals true Mercury, and straight sulfur, equally in imperfect as in perfect metals: It has only been made contaminated and impure in imperfect metals, and those which alone are deprived of perfect maturation. And for the same reasons they can be reduced to gold and silver, i.e., so that the impurity with which they had been defiled may be separated from the golden or silver nature that is in them, and the form of gold or silver may be instilled into them.
